questions.q: A TypeScript file imports "./vendor/naira-format/index.js" and tsc reports TS7016, "Could not find a declaration file for module". What does the compiler actually know about that module?
questions.explain: The message names the file it found. The project does not type-check JavaScript, and there is no index.d.ts beside it, so the imports would be implicitly any. Under strict (noImplicitAny) that is an error rather than a silent any.
options: Nothing: it could not find the file on disk
The JavaScript file exists, but the compiler has no types for it, so everything imported from it would be any
It has read the JavaScript and found a type error inside it
It knows the types, but the import path is missing an extension

questions.q: A developer silences TS7016 with // @ts-ignore above the import. What changes for the code that uses the library?
questions.explain: @ts-ignore adds no knowledge. With no declaration, the imported names are any, and any accepts every argument and every use of the result. That is how ₦2,500 became ₦25 in the lesson.
options: Nothing: the compiler still checks the calls, it only hides the one message
The compiler now reads the JavaScript file and infers its types
Every value imported from the library is any, so calls such as formatNaira("2500") are no longer checked
The import is removed from the emitted JavaScript

questions.q: Which statement about a .d.ts file is true?
questions.explain: A declaration file describes JavaScript that exists somewhere else. It emits nothing, and the JavaScript is still what runs. The compiler finds it by itself: next to the .js file, through the package's types, or in @types.
options: It is compiled into a small JavaScript file that checks the types at runtime
It contains only declarations (names and types, no function bodies) and produces no JavaScript
It must be imported explicitly in every file that uses the library
It replaces the JavaScript file, so the .js can be deleted

questions.q: A file imports "./lib/receipts.cjs". Which declaration file does the compiler look for first?
questions.explain: Declaration files mirror the JavaScript extension: .js goes with .d.ts, .mjs with .d.mts, and .cjs with .d.cts. The extension tells the compiler whether the module is CommonJS or ESM, so it must match.
options: ./lib/receipts.d.ts
./lib/receipts.d.cts
./lib/receipts.cts only
./types/receipts.d.ts

questions.q: A developer writes export declare function addVat(kobo: number): number { return kobo * 1.075; } in money.d.ts, and tsc with the course's usual settings reports nothing. Why?
questions.explain: An implementation in an ambient context is error TS1183, but skipLibCheck skips all declaration files, not only those in node_modules. Run tsc --skipLibCheck false whenever you change your own .d.ts files.
options: Function bodies are allowed in declaration files since TypeScript 5
The body is silently ignored, which is the intended behaviour
skipLibCheck: true skips type-checking every .d.ts file, including your own, so error TS1183 is never reported
declare turns the body into a runtime check

questions.q: What does this print when run with tsx, where no build step defines APP_VERSION?
questions.explain: The declaration emits nothing, so at runtime the name does not exist. typeof on an undeclared name is safe and gives "undefined"; reading it directly throws a ReferenceError. The compiler accepted both lines, because the declaration promised a string.
options:
undefined
ReferenceError

string
0

ReferenceError

TypeError

questions.q: What does the shorthand declare module "ms"; (no body) do?
questions.explain: A shorthand ambient module removes TS7016 by giving up all checking for that package. It is a temporary step during a migration, never the final fix.
options: Downloads the types for ms from DefinitelyTyped
Makes import ms from "ms" an error until you add a body
Declares the module so the import compiles, with every import from it typed any
Declares the module as having no exports

questions.q: This file stands in for code that uses an untyped duration library through a shorthand declaration (so parse is any). What does it print?
questions.explain: undefined * 2 is NaN, and every comparison with NaN is false. With any, the compiler allowed the arithmetic; a declaration returning number | undefined would have forced a check first.
options: NaN false
undefined false
0 false
TypeError: Cannot multiply undefined

questions.q: An untyped CommonJS package ends with module.exports = function slugify(text, options) { … }. How should its declare module block describe that?
questions.explain: export = is the declaration form of module.exports = …: the module is that value. An ES module then imports it as the default export (import slugify from "slugify"), as the lesson did with ms.
options: export default function slugify(…): string; only
Declare function slugify(…): string; and then export = slugify;
export const module = { exports: slugify };
export * from "slugify";

questions.q: types/ms.d.ts starts with import type { Options } from "./options.js"; and then has declare module "ms" { … }. What does the declare module block mean now?
questions.explain: A top-level import or export makes a file a module. Inside a module, declare module "name" augments an existing module instead of declaring a new one. For an untyped package with no declaration anywhere, that fails. Keep ambient module declarations in script files, and use import("./options.js").Options inside the block if you need another file's type.
options: The same as without the import: a new ambient module declaration
Because the file is now a module, it is an augmentation of an existing "ms" module, which must already resolve to a declaration
It is ignored, because declaration files cannot contain imports
It declares a global variable named ms

questions.q: Your application uses ms and you install @types/ms. Where does @types/ms belong in package.json?
questions.explain: Type packages are needed only to type-check and build. The exception is a library whose published .d.ts files refer to those types: its users need them too, so they go in dependencies.
options: devDependencies, because only the compiler uses it
dependencies, because ms is a dependency
peerDependencies, so the user chooses the version
Nowhere: @types packages are installed globally

questions.q: Your project depends on ms@2.1.3. Which @types/ms version describes it?
questions.explain: @types packages use the library's major and minor version, with their own patch number for fixes to the declarations. A mismatched major version may describe functions that do not exist in your copy of the library.
options: The newest @types/ms, whatever its version
A 2.1.x version: the major and minor numbers follow the library's
@types/ms@2.1.3 exactly, patch number included
Any version, because types do not change between releases

questions.q: You installed @types/ms, but an old types/ms.d.ts with declare module "ms" { … } is still in the project. What happens?
questions.explain: An ambient module declaration for the exact name is used before the compiler resolves the package. In the lesson, a local declaration made the "two hours" error from @types/ms disappear. Delete your own declaration when you install a real one.
options: The compiler reports a duplicate declaration error
The installed @types/ms wins, because it is in node_modules
The local ambient declaration is used for the import, so you keep your own (possibly weaker) types without any warning
The two declarations merge, and the stricter signature wins

questions.q: How do you tell that a package ships its own types, so no @types package is needed?
questions.explain: The compiler reads types and the "types" export condition. A package written in TypeScript still ships JavaScript; what matters is whether it also publishes the declarations. npm view <name> types exports shows the fields.
options: Its name starts with @
Its package.json has a "types" field, or "types" conditions inside "exports", pointing at .d.ts files
It has a tsconfig.json in its folder
It is written in TypeScript on GitHub

questions.q: A project's tsconfig.json has "types": ["node"]. You install @types/ms and write import ms from "ms". What happens?
questions.explain: types controls automatic inclusion of global declarations (like process from @types/node, or a test framework's global describe). Module imports are resolved normally, including node_modules/@types.
options: The import fails, because ms is not in the types list
The import works: the types list only limits which @types packages may add global names; imported packages are found regardless
The import works only after adding "ms" to types
The compiler ignores @types/ms but uses the JavaScript

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Here the declaration is backed by a real assignment on globalThis, so the global exists. var in declare global is what makes globalThis.visits a known property; let or const would not add it to globalThis.
options: 2 true
1 true
2 false
ReferenceError: visits is not defined

questions.q: Why does types/env.d.ts in the lesson end with export {};?
questions.explain: declare global is only allowed in a module. A file with any top-level import or export is a module, and export {} is the smallest one. (A script file could declare globals directly, without declare global.)
options: To export the ProcessEnv interface to other files
It exports nothing; it makes the file a module, which declare global { … } requires
To stop the file from being included by tsc
To make the environment variables available at runtime

questions.q: A team augments NodeJS.ProcessEnv with PAYSTACK_SECRET_KEY: string. What is the main risk?
questions.explain: The augmentation is a type-level promise with no runtime check. Keeping string | undefined and validating all variables once at startup gives a clear error at the right moment, and a typed configuration object for the rest of the program.
options: Node.js refuses to start when a declared variable is missing
The compiler now believes the variable is always a string, so a missing variable shows up later as a confusing undefined error deep inside the code
Other files can no longer read process.env
The secret is printed in the compiled JavaScript

questions.q: This simulates reading an environment variable that the compiler was told is always set. What does it print?
questions.explain: as string is the same kind of promise as a ProcessEnv augmentation. The value is still undefined, and calling a method on it throws a TypeError.

undefined
TypeError

string
false

false

questions.q: Two interfaces with the same name are declared in one file. What does this print?
questions.explain: Interfaces with the same name merge into one with all members, which is what module augmentation relies on. coupon is optional, so cart has only its id key at runtime. (Two type aliases with one name would be a duplicate identifier error.)
options: 1 id,coupon
2 id,coupon
1 id
The code does not compile: duplicate identifier 'Cart'

questions.q: In coupons.ts, declare module "./cart.js" { interface Cart { coupon?: … } } sits next to normal code. What does it do?
questions.explain: Module augmentation reopens an existing module's declarations. The merged interface is visible everywhere Cart is used. It changes types only; some code must still set coupon.
options: Declares a new module named ./cart.js that replaces the real one
Merges a coupon member into the Cart interface exported by the real cart.ts, for the whole project
Adds the coupon property to every cart object at runtime
Only affects the types inside coupons.ts

questions.q: An augmentation declare module "./carts.js" { … } fails with TS2664, "Invalid module name in augmentation". What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: An augmentation must name a module that the compiler can resolve, exactly as an import would. You can only add to something that exists.
options: Augmentations are only allowed for npm packages
The name does not resolve to an existing module (here, a typo for ./cart.js)
The file is missing export {}
Relative names must use .ts in augmentations

questions.q: A library exports export type Order = { id: string }. Can you add a field to Order with module augmentation?
questions.explain: Declaration merging works for interfaces, not for type aliases. That is why libraries that expect to be extended export interfaces for those extension points.
options: Yes, with declare module "lib" { type Order = { note?: string } }
No: type aliases do not merge, so a second Order is a duplicate identifier. Only interfaces (and namespaces) can be extended this way
Yes, but only with declare global
Yes, if you use interface Order extends Order

questions.q: This mimics an augmentation that declared a giftWrapFee function on a module that never defined it: the object's type claims the function exists. What does it print?
questions.explain: Types never create values. The type says giftWrapFee exists, the object does not have it, and calling it would throw "is not a function". An augmentation that declares new functions is the same lie across files.
options: 3500 undefined
3500 function
3500 number
The code does not compile

questions.q: A declaration claims parse always returns a number, but the implementation returns null for bad text. What does this print?
questions.explain: null + 500 is 500 in JavaScript, so the lie produced a plausible but wrong total with no error at all. Only a behaviour test that runs the real code would catch the declaration's missing | null.
options: null500
NaN
TypeError: Cannot add null

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: @ts-expect-error only silences the compiler. The line is still ordinary code and runs. That is why the lesson put type-only checks inside a function that is never called.
options: ran and threw: text.replace is not a function
type-only line skipped
ran and threw: Argument of type 'number' is not assignable
Nothing: the file does not compile

questions.q: You own an old JavaScript library with JSDoc comments such as @param {number} kobo. Which setup gives TypeScript users checked, generated declarations without rewriting it in TypeScript?
questions.explain: With allowJs the compiler reads JavaScript; with checkJs it checks the bodies against the JSDoc types; with declaration it writes declarations. The code and its declarations can no longer disagree.
options: Write a .d.ts by hand and keep it in sync
allowJs and checkJs to read and check the JavaScript against its JSDoc types, plus declaration (and emitDeclarationOnly) to write the .d.ts files
skipLibCheck: false
Rename every file from .js to .d.ts

questions.q: With declaration on, what does tsc write in the .d.ts for export let count = 0;?
questions.explain: A let can be reassigned, so its type is widened to number. For export const rate = 0.075 the compiler keeps the literal: export declare const rate = 0.075;.
options: export declare let count = 0;
export declare let count: number;
export declare const count: 0;
Nothing, because variables are not part of declarations

questions.q: With isolatedDeclarations on, which export is reported?
questions.explain: isolatedDeclarations requires every type that would have to be inferred from a body to be written out. A literal constant and an interface are clear from the text; loadOrder's return type can only be found by checking its body, so it needs an annotation.
options: export const VAT_RATE = 0.075;
export function total(items: number[]): number { … }
export async function loadOrder(id: string) { return { id, total: 5000 }; }
export interface Order { id: string }

questions.q: What does "declarationMap": true add for the users of your library?
questions.explain: A declaration map links positions in the .d.ts back to the .ts file. It helps readers of your code; sourceMap is the option for runtime stack traces.
options: Runtime source maps for stack traces
"Go to definition" in their editor jumps to your original .ts source instead of the .d.ts file (if the source is published)
A map of every exported name for tree shaking
Faster type checking of your package

questions.q: A package has no types and no @types package. You use two of its ten functions. What is the best first step?
questions.explain: Declare what you depend on, accurately. Files in node_modules are replaced on the next install. Later you can grow the declaration, or contribute it to DefinitelyTyped for everyone.
options: Add // @ts-ignore to each import
Declare the whole package with the shorthand declare module "pkg";
Write types/pkg.d.ts with a declare module "pkg" block that types the two functions you use, based on reading and running them
Edit node_modules/pkg to add an index.d.ts

questions.q: This implements the two jobs of an ms-style function with overloads. What does it print?
questions.explain: The overload signatures are what callers see; the last signature is the implementation and is hidden. Text is parsed into milliseconds, numbers are formatted, and text that does not match gives undefined, which the first overload admits honestly.
options: 900000 15m undefined
15m 900000 undefined
900000 900000m undefined

questions.q: A declaration says a legacy function returns { amount: number }, but it returns parsed JSON. What does this print?
questions.explain: The compiler believes amount is a number; the value is the string "2500", so + 100 concatenates. A declaration can describe data it cannot guarantee; validate data that comes from outside.
options: string 2500100
number 2600
string 2600
number 2500100

questions.q: You put types/ms.d.ts in your project, but the compiler still reports TS7016 for ms. The tsconfig.json has "include": ["src"]. What is wrong?
questions.explain: An ambient declaration only takes effect if its file is part of the program. With "include": ["src"], files outside src are ignored. Use "include": ["src", "types"], or keep the declaration inside src.
options: Declaration files must be named index.d.ts
The types folder is not included in the program, so the compiler never reads the declaration; add it to include
ms must be listed in the types option
Ambient declarations only work in node_modules/@types

questions.q: Write parseDuration with two overloads, like the ms declaration: given text such as "2h" or "30m" it returns milliseconds, or undefined if the text does not match; given a number of milliseconds it returns text in whole hours when possible ("2h"), otherwise whole minutes ("90m").
questions.explain: Two overload signatures tell callers exactly what each kind of argument returns, and the text overload admits undefined. The implementation signature underneath covers both and is not visible to callers.

questions.q: The declared type of discount says it returns a number of kobo, but the implementation was written by someone else. Write a behaviour check that calls it with each case and prints PASS or FAIL plus the case name, where a case passes only if the result is a whole, non-negative number equal to the expected value.
questions.explain: The type promised a whole number of kobo in every case. Running the real function shows a fraction (84,999.15) for an odd amount and null above 100%. Storing the result as unknown stops the (wrong) declared type from influencing the check.
questions.expected:
PASS 10% off ₦2,500
PASS no discount
FAIL 15% of an odd amount
FAIL more than 100%

questions.q: Instead of augmenting ProcessEnv, write readEnv(env) that takes a Record<string, string | undefined> and returns { nodeEnv: "development" | "production" | "test"; paystackKey: string }. NODE_ENV defaults to "development" and must be one of the three values; PAYSTACK_SECRET_KEY must start with "sk_". Throw one Error listing every problem, joined with "; ".
questions.explain: The types come out of checks, not promises: find returns a real NodeEnv or undefined, and the key is checked before it is returned as a string. The rest of the program receives a typed object and never touches process.env.

questions.q: Without editing the first Cart interface, add an optional coupon field of type { code: string; percentOff: number } by declaring a second interface with the same name, then make total apply the coupon (rounded to whole kobo).
questions.explain: The second interface Cart merges with the first, exactly as a module augmentation merges into another file's interface. Math.round keeps the result in whole kobo: 10% off ₦9,999.99 is 899,999.1 kobo before rounding.

questions.q: untyped stands for a JavaScript library you import as any. Write a typed wrapper formatKobo(kobo: number): string that refuses (throws a TypeError with the message "kobo must be a whole number") anything that is not a safe integer, then calls the library. The rest of the program should only use the wrapper.
questions.explain: A typed facade is the in-code cousin of a declaration file: the rest of the program sees a precise signature, and the one place that touches any checks both what goes in and what comes out. Number("2,500") is NaN, which is a number to the compiler but not a safe integer.

₦2500.00
TypeError: kobo must be a whole number
TypeError: kobo must be a whole number

questions.q: A test setup file must create a global requestCount that other files can use without an import. Declare it with declare global (remember which keyword makes a globalThis property), initialise it to 0 through globalThis, and make handle() increase it.
questions.explain: var inside declare global types a property of globalThis; the assignment makes it real. Without the assignment, the declaration would compile and requestCount += 1 would throw a ReferenceError.

questions.q: @types/ms hangs its helper types on the function with declare namespace ms. Here a real function and a namespace with the same name merge. What does this print?

A namespace merged with a function adds properties to that function, so slugify.separator exists and slugify is still a function. In a .d.ts file, declare namespace with only types adds nothing at runtime; it just gives types like ms.StringValue a home.

questions.explain: A top-level declare produces no JavaScript, so neither name exists at runtime. Declared functions have no body by design; the compiler only uses the signature.

exchangeRate: false, convert: true

questions.q: An untyped payments library returns unknown data that should look like { reference: string; kobo: number; status: "success" | "failed" }. Write the type guard isCharge(value: unknown): value is Charge that checks every field at runtime, so the rest of the code never has to trust a declaration.
questions.explain: A declaration file says what data should look like; a guard checks what it does look like. After isCharge returns true, the compiler narrows reply to Charge, and that narrowing is backed by real checks.
